overview.summary: Why homes cost so much: rival camps blame restricted supply, concentrated demand and inequality, or investor ownership — and each diagnosis dictates opposite fixes.
overview.scope_covered: Drivers of housing costs in rich-world cities: zoning and supply, demand and inequality, rent regulation and social housing, investor ownership, land taxation.
overview.scope_excluded: Homelessness services, mortgage finance and interest-rate cycles, construction technology and labor, rural land use; demand-restriction policies (immigration, foreign-buyer and second-home limits) as a distinct camp.
overview.why_now: The bipartisan ROAD to Housing Act, passed overwhelmingly in June 2026 with curbs on institutional purchases of single-family homes, put one camp's diagnosis into federal law while the others contest it.

basics.intro: First the scale of the problem, then the headline evidence behind each camp's diagnosis.

stats.label: Cost-burdened renters · share of renters
stats.note: A record 22.6 million US renter households (about half) spent 30%+ of income on housing in 2023.
stats.detail: The burden is sharply income-skewed: 83% of renters earning under $30,000 are cost-burdened versus 14% of those earning $75,000+, and roughly 12 million renters are severely burdened, paying over half their income on housing. 2023 marked the third consecutive record year.
stats.source_label: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies — State of the Nation's Housing 2025

stats.label: Housing unit shortage · US estimate
stats.note: Freddie Mac put the US undersupply at 3.7M homes as of Q3 2024; other estimates range 1.5–7M depending on method.
stats.detail: Estimates vary because there's no agreed equilibrium: Up for Growth found a 3.8M-unit shortfall (2025), Realtor.com found ~4.0M, and NLIHC estimates a 7.1M-unit gap specifically in housing affordable to extremely low-income renters. Some economists dispute that a uniform national shortage exists at all, arguing it is concentrated in specific metros and unit types rather than nationwide.

stats.label: House price-to-income growth · US since 2015
stats.note: The US price-to-income ratio is up ~31 index points since 2015, third-steepest among 36 OECD countries.
stats.detail: OECD's price-to-income index averaged 114.7 across 36 countries in 2024/25, but trajectories diverge sharply: Portugal (+53pts), Canada (+41pts) and the US (+31pts) saw the steepest run-ups since 2015, while 33 of 36 countries actually saw affordability improve in 2023–24 as wage growth outpaced home prices for the first time in a decade.

stats.label: Nearby rent change · after a new market-rate building opens
stats.note: New market-rate buildings (50+ units) cut nearby rents 5–7% within about two blocks over a few years, per an 11-city study.
stats.detail: Mast, Asquith & Reed's quasi-experimental study found new buildings also draw more in-migration from lower-income neighborhoods, with no local/regional supply tradeoff. A separate study complicates the picture at the very bottom: rents at the cheapest nearby buildings rose about 4% even as the priciest nearby buildings' rents fell, suggesting filtering benefits reach the top of the market faster than the bottom.

stats.label: Mega-landlord share · of investor-owned homes
stats.note: Investors owning 1,000+ homes hold about 2% of all investor-owned US homes, and were net sellers of single-family properties in 2024.
stats.detail: Overall investor purchases (individual plus institutional) hit 25.7% of 2024 home sales, the highest in five years — and small individual investors made a record ~59% of those investor purchases. Small investors also hold about 91% of the investor-owned housing stock. The largest institutional landlords — those owning 1,000 or more homes — hold roughly 2% of investor-owned homes and were net sellers of single-family properties in 2024, with some shifting toward purpose-built rental development instead of buying existing homes.
stats.source_label: CNBC / National Association of Realtors data

stats.label: Social/public housing share · selected systems
stats.note: Singapore's public housing (77% of residents) and Vienna's social housing (44% of stock) dwarf the US's public-housing sector (~1%).
stats.detail: The Netherlands sits in between, with the largest social-rental sector in Europe. Each figure reflects decades of sustained public investment and land banking rather than a short-term policy choice, and each carries distinct eligibility and tenure rules — Singapore's stock is majority owner-occupied, not rented, unlike Vienna's or the Netherlands'. Singapore's 77% is HDB's resident-population share (Singapore Department of Statistics/HDB); Vienna's 44% is the City of Vienna/Wiener Wohnen share of city rental stock; the Netherlands and US figures come from the OECD's PH4.2 social-rental-stock series.

stats.label: Zoning cost premium · share of home price above construction cost
stats.note: In supply-constrained metros, zoning premiums account for a large share of home prices — over 50% in San Francisco.
stats.detail: Glaeser and Gyourko's method infers the 'zoning tax' as the gap between home prices and physical construction cost. In most of the US this gap is small — prices track construction cost closely — but in a handful of tightly regulated coastal metros (also including New York, DC, Oakland and San Jose, each above 10%) it is the dominant driver of high prices.

stats.label: Rent reduction · Auckland after 2016 upzoning
stats.note: Auckland upzoned ~75% of its residential land in 2016; eight years on, rents were an estimated 23% lower than if it hadn't.
stats.detail: Using a synthetic-control method to build a counterfactual Auckland, researchers found rents were about 23% lower after eight years than they would have been without the 2016 reform. Attached-dwelling permits surged after upzoning, with roughly 127,000 new-dwelling permits issued citywide over 2017–2024, and the study attributes the rent decline to the added supply rather than to demand shifts alone — one of the clearest real-world tests of the supply-side thesis to date.

stats.label: Convergence in state incomes · annual rate
stats.note: Poor and rich US states' incomes converged 1.8%/year for a century; since 1990 the rate has fallen by more than half — a stall researchers tie to housing costs in high-wage metros.
stats.detail: Ganong & Shoag show that historically, low-income workers migrated to high-productivity places, closing wage gaps. Since the 1980s, tightening land-use regulation in high-income metros has raised housing costs enough that migration by less-skilled workers reversed, stalling convergence and linking local zoning rules to rising regional income inequality.

stats.label: Vacant buildings drop · Harrisburg under split-rate land tax
stats.note: Harrisburg cut vacant buildings from 4,000+ in the early 1980s to about 500 by 2001, after taxing land higher than buildings.
stats.detail: Pennsylvania's split-rate (two-rate) property tax lets cities tax land value higher than building value. Pittsburgh and Scranton saw construction booms not matched by neighboring cities after raising land tax rates in 1979–82, per tracking by economist Steven Cord. Detroit's mayor proposed a similar shift in 2023 — the enabling state legislation stalled — though these remain a handful of pilots that don't isolate the land tax from simultaneous local reforms.

stats.label: Homeownership rate · US households
stats.note: US homeownership sits at 65.6% (2024), roughly the same as in 1979 and below its 2004 peak of 69.2%.
stats.detail: The rate rose from 43.6% in 1940 to the mid-60s by the late 1970s, then climbed to a record 69.2% in 2004 during the subprime boom before falling after the 2008 crash. It has held roughly flat around 65–66% for the past decade, meaning about one in three US households rents rather than owns.

stats.label: Rent-regulated jurisdictions · US
stats.note: About 182 US cities/municipalities have rent control or stabilization, concentrated in CA, NY and NJ; 37 states ban it outright.
stats.detail: Coverage within regulated cities varies widely — roughly 44% of Washington DC's rental units fall under stabilization, and New York City has the largest stock of rent-regulated units in the country. There is no single tracked nationwide renter-coverage percentage; the policy remains a patchwork rather than a norm across the country.
stats.source_label: Rent control in the United States (legal tracking overview)

questions.text: Does adding market-rate housing lower rents nearby and metro-wide, and how fast does filtering reach low-income households?
questions.why: Supply Liberalizers say new homes free up older, cheaper ones as movers trade up — the 'filtering' chain; Demand-Side Skeptics and Tenant Decommodifiers say new luxury units sit atop the market for decades before touching the bottom, if ever.
questions.detail: The evidence landscape splits by geography and time horizon rather than by ideology alone: studies of metro-level rent trends tend to find that adding units — even high-end ones — loosens the whole local market by freeing up existing stock as movers vacate cheaper units, the classic 'filtering' chain. Skeptics don't dispute the chain exists; they dispute its speed and reach, arguing that in supply-constrained coastal metros the chain is too slow, too leaky (units get absorbed by in-migration or converted to short-term rentals), or breaks before reaching deeply low-income renters who need subsidized or below-market units, not merely 'less expensive market-rate' ones. The strongest liberalizer case rests on natural experiments where large permitting reforms preceded measurable rent deceleration; the strongest skeptic case rests on cities that built substantially and still saw affordability worsen because demand (income growth, in-migration, second-home buying) outpaced supply. Both camps agree filtering is real in principle — the fight is over magnitude, lag, and whether it's sufficient without complementary subsidy or regulation.

questions.text: How much of the price divergence across cities is explained by supply constraints versus demand, income growth, and inequality?
questions.why: This is the foundational disagreement beneath every other fight: if scarcity is manufactured by zoning, loosen it; if it's driven by income growth and inequality flowing into a fixed housing stock, supply fixes alone won't touch prices.
questions.detail: Supply Liberalizers point to the tightest correlation in the data: cities with the most restrictive zoning and permitting (height limits, minimum lot sizes, discretionary review) show the steepest long-run price growth relative to construction costs, and the divergence between elastic (easy-to-build) and inelastic (hard-to-build) metros widened for decades. Demand-Side Skeptics counter that the same high-cost metros are also the ones with the strongest income growth, most concentrated high-wage industries (tech, finance), and most acute inequality — so even substantial construction would only partly offset a demand shock. The honest complication is that these two forces are entangled rather than cleanly separable: restrictive zoning is often a response to demand pressure (rich, desirable cities zoning defensively), and cities that are demand magnets are also disproportionately the ones that restrict supply, making it hard to isolate one variable econometrically. Neither side denies the other factor exists; the dispute is about relative weight and, therefore, about whether supply-side reform alone can meaningfully close the affordability gap or whether it must be paired with redistribution.

questions.text: Do institutional investors and short-term rentals materially raise prices, or are they a symptom of underlying scarcity?
questions.why: Financialization Critics see investor buying and platforms like short-term rentals as an independent price driver worth regulating directly; Supply Liberalizers and Demand-Side Skeptics see it as downstream of scarcity.
questions.detail: The Financialization Critic case draws on the visibility of institutional single-family landlords and short-term rental conversion in specific hot markets, arguing that converting long-term housing stock into short-term rentals or algorithm-optimized rent-setting removes units from the resident supply and coordinates rent increases that wouldn't happen under fragmented mom-and-pop ownership. The counter-case, shared by Supply Liberalizers and Demand-Side Skeptics from different angles, is that investor ownership share is highest precisely in markets where scarcity (via restrictive zoning) or strong rental demand (via income growth) already makes housing a good investment — investors chase yield, they don't create it, and nationally institutional ownership remains a minority share of the rental stock even where locally visible. The genuinely contested middle ground is whether investor concentration has independent price effects at the margin (e.g., in specific submarkets or during specific buying sprees) even if it isn't the primary national driver — a claim that's harder to settle than either camp's headline framing suggests.

questions.text: Should housing be treated primarily as a market good or as a right partially insulated from market pricing?
questions.why: This is the values fork underneath the policy fights: whether affordability failures are market failures to fix within a market frame, or evidence that a baseline of housing should sit outside market allocation entirely.
questions.detail: This question can't be resolved by evidence because it's a disagreement about what housing is for. The market-good framing, closest to Supply Liberalizer and Georgist instincts, holds that treating housing like other scarce goods — letting price signals guide construction and letting supply respond to demand — is what has historically delivered abundant, affordable housing anywhere it's worked, and that deviations from market allocation (rent caps, exclusionary zoning) are themselves usually the cause of scarcity. The rights-based framing, closest to Tenant Decommodifier instincts, holds that shelter is a precondition for participating in society at all, not a discretionary consumer good, and that a market allocator will always underserve the bottom of the income distribution no matter how efficient it is — so some floor of decommodified housing (public, social, or deeply subsidized) is a moral requirement, not merely an efficiency question. Most real housing systems mix both framings (market-rate supply plus a public/social housing sector); the contested part is the size and permanence of the non-market floor, which is a values choice about acceptable levels of housing insecurity, not a factual dispute.

questions.text: Do rent freezes and controls protect tenants at an acceptable cost to new supply and maintenance of existing stock?
questions.why: Tenant Decommodifiers treat rent regulation as essential insurance against displacement; Supply Liberalizers treat it as the textbook policy that shrinks and degrades the very stock it's meant to protect.
questions.detail: The strongest tenant-side case is immediate and distributional: rent control demonstrably keeps existing covered tenants in place and shields them from the sharpest rent spikes and displacement, which matters enormously for household stability, especially for long-tenured renters. The strongest liberalizer case is structural and dynamic: economic research on rent control episodes has repeatedly found that covered units see landlords reduce maintenance investment, convert units to condos or owner-occupancy to exit regulation, and that new construction is disproportionately built outside a control regime's scope — shrinking the regulated stock and diverting investment toward higher-end unregulated housing over time. The real tension isn't whether rent control helps sitting tenants (it does, in the near term) but whether that benefit is worth the longer-run supply and quality costs, and whether modern 'second-generation' rent stabilization designs (vacancy decontrol, exemptions for new construction) can decouple the tenant-protection benefit from the supply-suppression cost — a design question rather than a yes/no verdict.

questions.text: Who should decide what gets built — existing residents through local control, or higher levels of government overriding them?
questions.why: This pits local democratic control (residents shaping their own neighborhood) against the claim that local vetoes externalize costs onto non-residents and future generations who have no vote in the process.
questions.detail: The local-control case is a democratic-legitimacy argument: people who live somewhere and pay its taxes have the strongest claim to decide its character, density, and infrastructure load, and centralizing land-use decisions strips accountability from the people most affected by day-to-day neighborhood change. The override case, favored by Supply Liberalizers and increasingly by some state-level reformers, is a collective-action argument: each locality's incentive is to restrict supply and export the regional consequences (higher prices, longer commutes, displaced workers) onto everyone else, so no single jurisdiction will voluntarily build its share of a metro's needed housing — making a higher level of government the only body positioned to weigh regional and future-resident interests that current local voters aren't incentivized to represent. This is fundamentally a values question about whose interests count in a land-use decision — current residents only, or the wider set of people who would live there if allowed to — dressed up in empirical-sounding debates about zoning outcomes.

questions.text: Would shifting property taxes from buildings onto land values spur construction and curb speculation without unacceptable transition costs?
questions.why: Georgist Land Taxers claim taxing land value instead of structures removes the penalty on building and punishes speculative land-banking; skeptics question whether the mechanism scales and who absorbs the transition shock.
questions.detail: The Georgist case is a mechanism argument: taxing land value rather than the building on top of it removes the current system's implicit penalty on improving property (since building more currently raises your tax bill), while making it costly to sit on vacant or underused land waiting for appreciation — in principle redirecting owners toward development rather than speculation, with the added appeal of taxing an inherently fixed, unproducible asset rather than productive investment. The skeptical case is about scale and transition: land value taxation has been implemented in only a few real-world jurisdictions at meaningful scale, so the confident causal claims about construction response are thinner than for zoning reform or rent control, where more natural experiments exist; and a shift onto land value could impose a sudden, large burden on asset-rich but cash-poor owners (long-time homeowners on valuable land) unless phased carefully. The genuinely open empirical question is less 'does the incentive direction make sense' — most economists across camps agree taxing land is efficient in theory — and more whether it would move construction enough in supply-constrained cities to matter, and whether transition design can avoid politically fatal shocks to existing owners.

positions.name: Supply Liberalizer
positions.steelman: Ban the ban: legalize enough homes and the affordability crisis ends.
positions.description:
Housing is expensive where it's illegal to build enough of it — full stop. We believe every family deserves the freedom to live near opportunity, and that freedom is being rationed by zoning codes, parking minimums, and permitting gauntlets that let incumbent homeowners veto their neighbors' homes. Legalize apartments, duplexes, and taller buildings, and construction responds, vacancy chains cascade down the income ladder, and rents fall for renters who never set foot in a new unit. This isn't theory: when Auckland upzoned three-quarters of its urban land in 2016, rents there were an estimated 23% lower eight years later than in similar New Zealand cities that didn't reform (Greenaway-McGrevy & So, Economic Inquiry 2025), and a 2025 Pew Charitable Trusts analysis of 1,654 U.S. zip codes found every 10% jump in local housing supply cut rent growth by 1.4 points, with the biggest relief flowing to the oldest, cheapest units. The mechanism — filtering — is exactly what abundance requires: build for the top of the market and openings ripple downward.

Sources:
- [Auckland upzoning reduced rents ~23% after eight years — Greenaway-McGrevy & So (Economic Inquiry, 2025)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ecin.70075)
- [Pew: New housing slows rent growth most for older, more affordable units (2025)](https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2025/07/31/new-housing-slows-rent-growth-most-for-older-more-affordable-units)
positions.detail: The intellectual roots trace to Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko's 2002 NBER paper "Zoning's Steep Price," which first showed home prices in coastal and Northeastern metros had decoupled from construction costs — the gap, they argued, was a "zoning tax." Their 2005 follow-up with Raven Saks split growing U.S. metros into supply-elastic and supply-constrained camps, and a 2024 update found the constraint has since spread to previously fast-building Sunbelt cities like Austin and Nashville, which is why the movement now treats state-level preemption of local zoning (as California, Oregon, and Montana have done) as necessary, not optional — city councils captured by incumbent homeowners won't deregulate themselves. Internally, the debate is about sequencing and reach: filtering purists argue any new supply helps, even luxury condos, because it removes a rich household from the used-housing pool; others (e.g., California YIMBY's affordable-housing carve-outs) argue market-rate legalization must be paired with subsidy or inclusionary requirements to reach the bottom decile fast enough, since filtering can take years to cascade. Skeptics point to the small, immediate effect size of any single building; proponents reply with the Auckland and Pew results precisely because they measure metro-wide and neighborhood-wide effects, not one building's tenants — the claim was never that new construction fills with poor people, but that it drains demand off the entire stock. The 2025 book "Abundance" by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson mainstreamed the argument beyond economists, framing permitting delay and litigation (not just zoning maps) as liberal governance's self-inflicted wound.
positions.proponents: Edward Glaeser, Joseph Gyourko, Bryan Caplan, California YIMBY, YIMBY Action, Ryan Greenaway-McGrevy, Ezra Klein, Derek Thompson
positions.representative_note: Harvard economist; "Zoning's Steep Price" (2002, with Gyourko) is the founding empirical text of the YIMBY case

positions.name: Financialization Critic
positions.steelman: Wall Street turned shelter into an asset class — break its grip before you touch zoning.
positions.description: Housing is first a place to live, not a yield-bearing instrument, and the last two decades bent the market the wrong way: after 2008, private equity and REITs (real estate investment trusts) bought up hundreds of thousands of single-family homes and turned tenants into a captive income stream. The clearest proof isn't abstract — it's RealPage, whose pricing software let competing landlords share nonpublic rent data to coordinate above-market rents, which is why the DOJ and eight state AGs sued it and why, in November 2025, RealPage agreed to stop using real-time competitor data and restrict pricing algorithms to data at least a year old. In metro Phoenix, 70% of apartment units were priced through software using that shared data, and Greystar's RealPage-managed portfolio "outperformed the market" on rent growth even during a downturn — that's not a free market, it's coordinated pricing dressed up as software. Short-term rentals compound it: peer-reviewed studies from Los Angeles to Barcelona to Berlin find Airbnb-style listings measurably raise rents and prices by converting long-term housing stock into tourist yield. Building more supply without curbing who owns it and how they price it just hands financial landlords a bigger asset base to extract from.
positions.detail: The framework traces to scholars like Desiree Fields and Manuel Aalbers, who after the 2008 foreclosure crisis documented how private equity firms (Blackstone's Invitation Homes chief among them) bought distressed single-family homes in bulk and packaged the rents into securities — turning housing into "yield," not shelter. That thesis hardened into policy once RealPage's algorithm became public: the DOJ's 2024 antitrust suit alleged the software let landlords who compete on paper share confidential rent and occupancy data to coordinate pricing, and the November 2025 settlement forcing RealPage to drop real-time data and impose a one-year lag on inputs is treated here as vindication — proof the "free market" story was covering for a cartel. Proponents include tenant unions organizing under the new Tenant Union Federation (Kansas City, Louisville, Chicago, Connecticut, Bozeman), the Private Equity Stakeholder Project's "Wall Street Landlords" tracking work, and legislators like Sen. Jeff Merkley and Sen. Sherrod Brown, who've pushed bills (the End Hedge Fund Control of American Homes Act and similar) to cap or unwind institutional single-family holdings. The internal debate is over how big the problem actually is: institutional investors (1,000+ home portfolios) still hold roughly 0.35% of the single-family stock nationally, which critics on their own side admit undercuts a "Wall Street owns your street" framing — so the sharper current argument leans less on aggregate ownership share and more on concentration in specific metro rental markets (Phoenix, Atlanta, Charlotte) and on algorithmic price coordination, where the RealPage case gives a hard evidentiary win, plus the STR literature (LA, Barcelona, Berlin) showing measurable rent and price effects from converting long-term stock to short-term yield.
positions.proponents: Desiree Fields, Manuel Aalbers, Private Equity Stakeholder Project, Tenant Union Federation, Sen. Jeff Merkley, Sen. Sherrod Brown, U.S. Department of Justice Antitrust Division (RealPage litigation)
positions.representative_note: Geographer whose research established the "financialization of rental housing" framework tracing how post-2008 private equity buyouts (Blackstone/Invitation Homes) turned single-family rentals into securitized yield instruments — the analytic base the RealPage antitrust case is read as confirming.

positions.name: Tenant Decommodifier
positions.steelman: A home is a right, not an asset — decommodify it and the market stops deciding who stays.
positions.description: Housing exists to shelter people, not to generate returns — so long as it's left to the market, it will be built and priced for whoever can pay most, not for whoever needs it most. Even record construction hasn't closed the gap: the National Low Income Housing Coalition puts the U.S. shortfall of rental homes affordable and available to extremely low-income renters at more than 7 million units, a deficit that new market-rate supply structurally cannot reach because it isn't profitable to build for that income tier. The fix is to pull housing out of the speculative market: rent stabilization, strong tenant protections, and public and social housing at real scale. Vienna is the proof of concept — roughly 60% of residents live in city-owned or subsidized housing (including limited-profit cooperatives beyond the ~44% municipal rental stock cited in Basics), and that scale keeps average rents near €10/m², a fraction of market-rate peer cities. Stability itself is the point as much as price: research links rent stabilization to fewer evictions and to gains in tenant health, school performance, and community stability that a purely price-focused fix would miss.
positions.detail: The intellectual root is Karl Polanyi's idea of housing as a "fictitious commodity" — something markets can price but were never designed to allocate justly — updated for the present crisis in Peter Marcuse and David Madden's "In Defense of Housing" (2016), which argues the crisis is a crisis of commodification itself, not a shortage to be engineered away by more market supply. The living model is interwar "Red Vienna," which built municipal housing outside the market on principle and never stopped; today's Gemeindebau and limited-profit cooperatives cover a majority of Viennese residents specifically because the program stayed universal rather than means-tested, avoiding the stigma and political fragility that hollowed out means-tested U.S. public housing under disinvestment and HOPE VI demolition. That history feeds a live internal debate: universal, broad-based social housing (Vienna, Singapore) builds durable middle-class political support, while targeted low-income public housing is easier to fund short-term but easier to starve later — most tenant organizers now favor the universal model precisely for its political durability, even where it costs more upfront. A second internal debate is means versus ends: some wings (DSA's "abolish rent" current, tenant unions organizing under labor-law frameworks) prioritize building tenant power and collective bargaining over any single policy instrument, on the view that stabilization and public housing without organized tenants get rolled back, as U.S. public housing was. On the evidence question, proponents don't rest on any single contested study: an Urban Institute/NLIHC review finds rent stabilization reforms associated with net increases in units affordable to extremely low-income renters even amid a reduction in the overall unit count, and a University of Minnesota study of "good cause" eviction protections found no evidence they slow new housing development — directly rebutting the standard supply-side objection. The financialization strand (Manuel Aalbers, Desiree Fields) adds that institutional ownership and algorithmic rent-setting are accelerants layered on top of an already-commodified system, meaning even a supply fix leaves the underlying vulnerability — that shelter is priced as an investment — untouched.
positions.proponents: Peter Marcuse, David Madden, Samuel Stein, Leilani Farha (The Shift), Manuel Aalbers, Desiree Fields, National Low Income Housing Coalition, Democratic Socialists of America housing platform, Right to the City Alliance, Tenants Together, City of Vienna (Wiener Wohnen)
positions.representative_name: In Defense of Housing (David Madden & Peter Marcuse, 2016) / Vienna's Gemeindebau model
positions.representative_note: Madden and Marcuse's book is the movement's foundational text, framing the crisis as one of commodification rather than scarcity; Vienna's century-old universal municipal housing program, still housing roughly 60% of residents, is the proponents' standing proof that decommodified housing can operate at metropolitan scale.

positions.name: Demand-Side Skeptic
positions.steelman: The crisis is who can pay, not what's allowed to be built.
positions.description: Housing markets are working exactly as markets do: prices track the purchasing power of the households bidding, and for forty years that power has pulled apart. A 2026 empirical simulation by Buchholz, Kemeny, Randolph and Storper found that even a dramatic, deregulation-driven supply expansion would take decades to generate widespread affordability in America's high-cost metros — because uneven demand growth from rising interpersonal and interregional inequality is the primary driver of declining affordability, not the permitting queue. Gyourko, Mayer and Sinai's "superstar cities" research already showed this mechanism at the metro level: from 1950–2000, an expanding population of high-income, high-willingness-to-pay households bid up land in supply-constrained coastal cities faster than construction ever could absorb, pricing out lower earners regardless of how much got built. Filtering is real but glacially slow and geographically narrow — new luxury units free up mid-tier stock only after a chain of moves that can take a decade to reach the bottom of the market, by which point wage stagnation and asset-price inflation have moved the target. Fix the income and wealth distribution — through wages, transfers, and taxation — and you fix the demand curve driving prices up; fixate on zoning maps alone and you're rearranging deck chairs on a ship whose passengers keep getting richer relative to each other.
positions.detail: This position emerged as a direct rebuttal to the "just build more" consensus that dominated US and UK housing debate through the 2010s. Its intellectual roots go back to Gyourko, Mayer and Sinai's 2013 "Superstar Cities" (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy), which modeled how a national rightward shift in the income distribution — not local land-use rules per se — explains why house-price appreciation in San Francisco, New York, and Boston diverged so sharply from the median American metro. Ganong and Shoag's NBER work extended the logic to migration: rising housing costs in high-income places have redirected low-skill migration away from exactly the labor markets that could raise their wages, and the authors calculate this stalled convergence explains roughly 10% of the rise in US wage inequality since 1980 — evidence that housing cost divergence and income inequality are locked in a mutually reinforcing spiral, not a one-way street from zoning to price. The position sharpened into open conflict with supply-side YIMBY economics via Buchholz, Kemeny, Randolph and Storper's 2026 paper (SocArXiv/LSE), whose empirical simulation directly challenges the "elastic supply would fix this" claim by modeling how long deregulated construction would actually take to reach broad affordability — their answer: decades, because demand from an increasingly unequal, increasingly geographically sorted set of high earners keeps refilling the gap as fast as units are added. Internationally, Cameron Murray's "The Great Housing Hijack" (2024) supplies the sharpest version of the filtering critique from Australia, arguing developers strategically release supply to protect absorption rates rather than flood markets, so added zoning capacity doesn't mechanically translate into faster or deeper price declines. The internal debate within this camp is over remedy: some proponents favor wage and welfare-state interventions (housing vouchers, EITC-style transfers, minimum wage) to address purchasing power directly, while others favor progressive taxation of the wealth gains that housing itself has generated for existing owners — but all agree the diagnostic error of the supply-liberalizer camp is treating a distributional problem as a production problem.
positions.proponents: Michael Storper, Tom Kemeny, Gregory Randolph, Maximilian Buchholz, Peter Ganong, Daniel Shoag, Cameron Murray
positions.representative_note: "Inequality, not regulation, drives America's housing affordability crisis" (SocArXiv/LSE) — the empirical simulation showing deregulated supply expansion would take decades to restore affordability, because uneven demand growth from rising inequality is the primary driver of the crisis.

positions.name: Georgist Land Taxer
positions.steelman: Tax the location, not the home — you can't offshore land or dodge a tax on hoarding it.
positions.description:
Land's value comes from the community around it — the transit line, the school, the jobs, the crowd — not from anything the owner built, so that value belongs to the public, not to whoever happens to hold the deed. A land value tax (LVT) captures that unearned gain instead of taxing the walls and roof people actually build, which means it can't be passed through in higher rents or dodged by leaving a lot vacant, and it makes speculation on empty and underused parcels expensive rather than free. This isn't a fringe idea: Pennsylvania cities that shifted to split-rate taxes saw a real construction response — McKeesport's building-permit value jumped 36% in the three years after its 1980 switch while neighboring Clairton, which didn't switch, fell 30%. Detroit's 2022-23 land-tax study, commissioned by the city and backed by the Kresge Foundation, found the reform would cut bills for 97% of homeowners by an average of 17-27%, funded by finally taxing the empty lots and surface parking lots speculators are sitting on. Economists across the spectrum — Milton Friedman called it "the least bad tax" — agree it's the one tax that doesn't shrink the thing you tax, because the supply of land is fixed no matter the rate.

Sources: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, "Split-Rate Property Taxation in Detroit" (lincolninst.edu, accessed 2026-07-11); City of Detroit, "Land Value Tax Plan" and Kresge Foundation-funded 2022 study summary (detroitmi.gov, kresge.org, accessed 2026-07-11); Lars Doucet, "Land Is a Big Deal" and Astral Codex Ten "Does Georgism Work?" series (landisabigdeal.com, astralcodexten.com, accessed 2026-07-11).
positions.detail: The idea traces to Henry George's 1879 "Progress and Poverty," which asked why poverty deepens alongside progress and answered: because rising land values are captured privately while labor and capital bear the tax burden. George's "single tax" movement shaped early 20th-century reform (it influenced the design of Monopoly, ironically, as an anti-monopoly teaching tool) before fading from mainstream politics for decades. It resurfaced through a tech-adjacent revival led by Lars Doucet, whose viral Astral Codex Ten book review of "Progress and Poverty" and subsequent book "Land Is a Big Deal" reframed the modern housing crisis as George's problem returned — and in February 2025 Doucet and Greg Miller founded the Center for Land Economics, a nonprofit dedicated to LVT policy and research. Internally, Georgists debate how "pure" a land tax must be to count: full-throated advocates want land value assessed and taxed at close to 100%, funding a citizen's dividend or replacing other taxes entirely, while pragmatists back "split-rate" taxation — a lower rate on buildings, higher on land — as the achievable on-ramp, since it doesn't require abolishing existing property tax systems overnight. The strongest evidence is the Pennsylvania natural experiment: roughly 15-20 municipalities adopted split-rate taxes over the 20th century, and studies (including Lincoln Institute analyses) found statistically significant increases in building-permit activity and property values after adoption compared to non-adopting neighbors. Detroit's 2022 study (from a 2019-commissioned effort backed by Invest Detroit and Kresge) modeled a land-tax rate more than double the building rate — 189 mills on land versus a 14-mill cut on structures — and found it would cut property tax delinquency and foreclosure risk while raising costs on the city's thousands of vacant and speculatively-held parcels; the plan required Michigan enabling legislation (House Bills 4966-4970), which stalled in the legislature — a 2023 House vote deadlocked 50-50 — so the city ballot measure originally planned for 2023-24 never took place. Critics counter that land value is hard to assess separately from buildings, that a big one-time tax hike on land could hit some legacy owners (churches, long-held family land) even if aggregate homeowners win, and that few big cities have tried a full-strength version — Georgists reply that Pennsylvania and the Detroit modeling are exactly the proof-of-concept at the scale that matters, and that assessment technology (GIS, sales-comparison modeling) has solved the "can't separate land from buildings" problem that stalled LVT a century ago. Milton Friedman and Joseph Stiglitz have each separately endorsed land-value taxation's efficiency case, cross-spectrum validation the movement cites despite neither being a Georgist proponent.
positions.proponents: Henry George, Lars Doucet, Center for Land Economics (Doucet and Greg Miller), Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan (proposer)
positions.representative_name: Lars Doucet / Center for Land Economics
positions.representative_note: Author of "Land Is a Big Deal" and co-founder (Feb 2025) of the Center for Land Economics, the leading present-day think tank translating Georgist land-value-tax theory into concrete municipal policy.

crux.lead: Are homes scarce because we banned building — or expensive because we turned them into investments?
crux.lead_highlight: or expensive because we turned them into investments?
crux.subtitle: One crisis, three diagnoses: banned building, concentrated buying power, or the business model.
crux.empirical: Whether new market-rate supply actually lowers rents nearby and metro-wide, and how far down the income ladder filtering reaches — and how fast — before income growth, inequality, and investor demand absorb it. Upzoning natural experiments and building-level rent studies cut one way; price-to-income divergence across cities cuts the other.
crux.values: Whether housing should be a market good and a household's wealth vehicle at all, or a right partially insulated from pricing — and who gets to decide what is built: existing residents through local control, tenants through collective power, or higher governments overriding both. No filtering study settles whether a home may double as someone's asset.

notes: Crux lead binarizes the debate to two camps (supply restriction vs financialization) — 'banned building or turned them into investments' — leaving the Demand-Side Skeptic's inequality diagnosis out of the headline framing even though its prevalence_weight (45) is close to the Financialization Critic's (60). The empirical crux body does include income growth/inequality, so no reader is misled, but a three-way lead (or folding inequality into the second clause) would better reflect the position set.

The 'Institutional investor share · 2%' basics stat is the only basics entry touching the Financialization camp, and its note/detail lean rebuttal-flavored ('dwarfed by small investors', 'actually retreating') rather than descriptive. The camp's own strongest numbers (25.7% overall investor purchase share, RealPage/Phoenix algorithmic-pricing coverage) appear only in the detail or the position card. Consider a more neutral note phrasing or promoting the 25.7% overall-investor figure to the headline value with the 2% institutional split in the detail — the current framing is accurate and the position card carries the camp's case, so this does not mislead, but it is the one basics entry that reads as arguing with a camp rather than informing.

Basics evidentiary weight skews supply-side (zoning premium, new-building rent effect, Auckland, Ganong-Shoag) with no equivalent headline stat for the Demand-Side Skeptic's core claim (e.g., a superstar-cities price-vs-income divergence figure beyond the OECD index). This mostly reflects the real literature's asymmetry, which the editorial rules permit, but one demand-side-native stat would tighten parity.

Action counts are slightly uneven: Supply Liberalizer and Tenant Decommodifier get two actions each (learn + volunteer), while Financialization Critic, Demand-Side Skeptic, and Georgist get one. Not misleading, but easy to even out.

Question 6's closing phrase 'dressed up in empirical-sounding debates' is mildly dismissive of both sides' empirical framing; a flatter phrasing ('though it is often argued in empirical terms') would keep the same point without the edge.

Georgist and Tenant Decommodifier steelman lines run past the ~90-char banner target (~110 and ~100 chars); the distribution stage can trim, e.g. 'Tax the location, not the home — you can't dodge a tax on land you're sitting on.'

Joseph Gyourko appears as a proponent of both Supply Liberalizer (zoning tax) and Demand-Side Skeptic (superstar cities). Both attributions are accurate to his work, but listing the same economist in opposing camps may confuse readers — consider dropping Gyourko/Mayer/Sinai from the Skeptic proponent list and keeping them only in its detail text as intellectual roots.
Tenant Decommodifier's representative_name contains an HTML entity ('Madden & Marcuse') and names a book/model rather than a person, unlike the other four positions — normalize for consistency.
Financialization Critic's description ends without the 'Sources:' link block that Supply Liberalizer and Georgist have; the claims are sourced in detail/basics, but format parity would be nice.

The localist/homeowner (NIMBY) perspective exists only inside the 'who should decide' question; that placement is defensible since it isn't a cost diagnosis, but worth a conscious editorial confirmation.

blocking.issue: Cost-burdened renters stat is misattributed and one detail is wrong. The figures (22.6M renter households, half of renters, 83% of <$30k renters, ~12.1M severely burdened, 2023 data) come from JCHS's State of the Nation's Housing 2025 — the cited report, America's Rental Housing 2024 (https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/americas-rental-housing-2024), reports 22.4M in 2022. Also, JCHS/NLIHC describe 2023 as the THIRD consecutive record year, not the fourth.
blocking.fix: Change source to JCHS State of the Nation's Housing 2025 (e.g. https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/housing-cost-burdens-climb-record-levels-again-2023 or the SOTN 2025 report page), source_published '2025 (data 2023)'; change 'fourth consecutive record year' to 'third'; use 12.1M for severely burdened.

blocking.issue: Institutional-investor stat is mis-stated on two axes versus its cited source. The CNBC/BatchData article says investors owning 1,000+ properties account for ~2% of investor-OWNED homes (a stock share) and are net sellers; it does not say institutions with '100+ homes' bought 'under 2% of US home sales in 2024' (a purchase-flow share with a different threshold). The 25.7%-of-2024-sales and ~91% small-investor (1-5 props 87% + 6-10 props 4% of investor-owned homes) figures do check out.
blocking.fix: Restate the stat to match the source: 'Investors owning 1,000+ homes hold about 2% of investor-owned homes and have been net sellers', citing CNBC/BatchData — or, if a purchases-share framing is wanted, find and cite a source that actually measures institutional share of purchases (e.g. Realtor.com/Parcl Labs) and use its threshold.

blocking.issue: Zoning-premium stat is misattributed. The city-level shares (SF 50%+, LA ~34%, Boston ~19% of house value as 'zoning tax') are from Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005), 'Why Have Housing Prices Gone Up?' — verified they do NOT appear in the cited 2003 FRBNY paper (I downloaded the PDF; its tables are hedonic land prices and regressions, no per-city zoning-tax-share percentages).
blocking.fix: Point source_url to the 2005 paper, e.g. https://www.hks.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/centers/taubman/files/Glaeser_05_PricesGoneUp.pdf (or the Stanford mirror), source_label 'Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (AER 2005)', source_published '2005 (1999-2000 data)'.

blocking.issue: Wrong proponent name in the Supply Liberalizer detail: 'their 2005 follow-up with Albert Saks' — the co-author is Raven Saks (Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks).

notes: Verified accurate: Freddie Mac 3.7M shortage (Nov 2024, Q3 2024 data, page live); NLIHC 7.1M gap; Pew 2025 study (1,654 zip codes, 10% supply -> 1.4pts lower rent growth); Auckland upzoning ~28% rent effect and both URLs (Cowles + Auckland EPC PDF) live; Ganong & Shoag 1.8%/yr convergence, NBER PDF live; Buchholz/Kemeny/Randolph/Storper 2026 LSE III working paper exists and is characterized fairly; RealPage DOJ proposed settlement (Nov 24, 2025: 12-month-old data, no real-time competitor data) confirmed; Phoenix 70% figure confirmed (Arizona AG suit); investor 25.7% of 2024 sales confirmed; homeownership 65.6% and 69.2% peak correct; ROAD to Housing Act passed Senate 85-5 / House 358-32 in June 2026 with 350-home institutional purchase restriction — confirmed.

why_now could be sharpened: the Act became law TODAY (July 11, 2026) without the President's signature after passing in June — 'passed overwhelmingly in June 2026' is accurate but the just-became-law fact is stronger and the investor threshold is 350 homes.
RealPage settlement is a PROPOSED consent decree pending court approval, with no admission of wrongdoing — 'agreed to stop' is fine but consider 'agreed in a proposed settlement'.

Phoenix 70% is strictly 'units owned/operated/managed by companies contracted with RealPage' (Arizona AG complaint), slightly broader than 'priced through software using that shared data' — soften a notch.

Supply Liberalizer detail calls the 2002 NBER paper 'Zoning's Steep Price'; the NBER WP (w8835) is titled 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' — 'Zoning's Steep Price' was the Regulation magazine version. Minor title conflation.

Rent-control stat cites Wikipedia; the ~182-jurisdictions figure originates with NMHC/Urban Institute tracking — a primary tracker (e.g. NMHC rent-control map or Urban Institute) would be a stronger citation for a tier-3 stat.

Financialization Critic detail's 'roughly 0.35% of the single-family stock' held by 1,000+ portfolios — most estimates land at ~0.4-0.6% (roughly 450-500k homes); consider 'roughly half a percent' or cite a specific tracker (Urban Institute).
Vienna 44% / Netherlands 30% ranked stat cites the OECD PH4.2 national dataset, which won't contain a Vienna city figure; consider adding a City of Vienna source alongside OECD.

URL health: all 19 source/action URLs are live. JCHS, Pew, OECD indicator page, and FRED return 403/000 to curl due to bot-blocking, but all four pages are confirmed live via search/cache; CNBC, Auckland PDF, OECD PDF, Lincoln Institute, NBER, NY Fed, Upjohn, PESP, Homes Guarantee, Tenant Federation, Groundwork, Local Housing Solutions, and both YIMBY Action pages return 200.

The lead's binary ('banned building' vs 'turned them into investments') maps to the Supply Liberalizer and Financialization/Decommodifier poles but skips the Demand-Side Skeptic diagnosis (inequality and purchasing power), which the draft itself calls 'the foundational disagreement' in question 2. The empirical crux text does fold inequality back in ('before income growth, inequality, and investor demand absorb it'), so readers aren't ultimately misled — but a lead that gestured at all three diagnoses (e.g. '...or expensive because the buyers got richer?') would narrow more faithfully. Note-level, not blocking, since the crux body carries the full disagreement.

Subtitle 'they split on whether scarcity is the cause or the business model' has the same two-camp compression; consider 'whether scarcity, unequal demand, or the business model is the cause' if it fits the register.

The values crux is genuinely a values fork (commodity vs right, plus who decides) with no verdict — good. One small addition that would sharpen it: the Georgist camp's distinctive values claim (land value is community-created and publicly owed) isn't reflected in either crux axis, though at prevalence 25 this is a defensible omission.
No house verdict anywhere in the crux; the empirical paragraph's 'cut one way / cut the other' construction is a good model of honest non-balance rather than 'both sides have a point' filler.

Crux subtitle ('they split on whether scarcity is the cause or the business model') compresses five camps into a two-way split that excludes the Demand-Side Skeptic diagnosis (inequality/purchasing power, neither scarcity-by-ban nor financialization). Not blocking because that camp's steelman ('The crisis is who can pay, not what's allowed to be built') and Q2 sit above the fold and correct the picture — but consider rewording the subtitle to a three-way fork, e.g. '...split on whether the cause is banned building, concentrated purchasing power, or the business model.'

Institutional investor stat: the record 25.7% TOTAL investor share of 2024 purchases lives only in the detail field. The compact note is honest ('under 2%... dwarfed by small investors') and Q3's why presents both readings, but a reader can't gauge the overall investor footprint from the compact layer; consider working the ~26% total into the note if it fits.

Zoning cost premium stat: the detail-only caveats that (a) in most of the US the price/construction-cost gap is small and (b) the underlying data is from 1999 are load-bearing for calibration. The note's 'In supply-constrained metros' scoping mostly covers (a); (b) is visible only if the source_published line ('2003 (1999 data)') renders on the card — worth confirming it does.

Nearby rent change stat: the complication that the cheapest nearby buildings' rents ROSE ~4% is detail-only. Compensated above the fold by Q1's why carrying the skeptic filtering critique, so noted rather than blocking.

Price-to-income stat: the detail-only fact that 33 of 36 countries saw affordability improve in 2023-24 is a meaningful counter-trend, but the note's explicit 'since 2015' window keeps the compact line honest.

Question T1 'Does adding market-rate housing lower rents…' uses the term of art 'filtering' in the compact question text; the adjacent 'why' does define it ('new homes free up older, cheaper ones as movers trade up'), so it clears the bar, but moving the plain gloss into the question text itself (e.g. 'how fast do freed-up older homes reach low-income households') would be cleaner.

Stat 'House price-to-income growth': value/unit reads '31 pts' while the note says 'grown about 31% faster than incomes' — pts vs % is a minor register mismatch a general reader may stumble on; consider aligning the unit with the note's phrasing.
Stat 'Housing unit shortage' detail uses the bare acronym 'NLIHC'; expanded register allows terms of art but asks for definition at first use — spell out National Low Income Housing Coalition once.

Action titles 'YIMBY Action: Legalize Housing' and 'Join a YIMBY Action chapter' carry the acronym YIMBY undefined; it is an organization's proper name so it passes, but nothing in any compact field ever glosses it ('yes in my backyard') — a one-word gloss in one of the two action descriptions would help.

Position steelmen for 'Tenant Decommodifier' ('decommodify it and the market stops deciding who stays') and 'Georgist Land Taxer' lean on movement vocabulary, but each steelman's surrounding clause supplies the plain meaning ('a home is a right, not an asset'; 'tax the location, not the home'), so both clear the compact bar.

Stat 'Zoning cost premium': the compact note largely restates the label ('zoning premiums account for a large share of home prices') plus the SF figure; the note could carry one more retainable anchor (e.g. that in most of the US the premium is near zero), which the detail currently holds alone. Non-blocking since the ranked series carries the numbers.

All 12 stat details and all 7 question details genuinely add mechanism, precision, or sourcing over their compact lines — no restatement cases found. Crux if-empirical/if-values also add over the lead/subtitle.

Basics tier-1 set is well-chosen: one scale stat (cost-burdened renters) plus one headline evidence stat per major camp (shortage + nearby-rent for supply, price-to-income for demand, investor share for financialization, social-housing share for decommodifiers), and the 7th above-fold slot going to the T2 zoning premium is a defensible pick given the crux centers on supply constraints.

Mild camp asymmetry above the fold: four of five positions have their signature stat visible, but the Georgist camp's evidence (Harrisburg split-rate, T2) sits below the fold while three supply-leaning stats (shortage, nearby rent change, zoning premium) show. This is consistent with the camp's low prevalence weight (25) and its T3 question, so it reads as honest non-balance rather than tilt — but if you ever want tighter camp coverage above the fold, swapping Harrisburg for the convergence stat's below-fold slot ordering would be the lever, not a promotion to T1.

Auckland 28% (T2, below fold) is arguably stronger supply evidence than the T1 'nearby rent change' stat — a metro-wide natural experiment vs a two-block hyperlocal effect. Keeping only one filtering stat above the fold is fine; if the fold ever tightens to 6, Auckland vs nearby-rent is worth revisiting since the Supply Liberalizer steelman leads with Auckland.

Questions tier-1 set matches the crux exactly (filtering, supply-vs-demand weight, investors, market-good-vs-right) — the right four. Rent control (T2) is the most publicly salient debate left below the fold, but it is genuinely downstream of the market-good-vs-right question that IS above the fold, so the drop-off is real.
Positions 5/5 above fold with all T1 is correct for a 5-camp topic; no marginal camp is padding the set.

plan_positions.name: Supply Liberalizer
plan_positions.sketch: Zoning and permitting caps on building are the root cause; legalize more homes and prices fall for everyone through filtering.

plan_positions.name: Financialization Critic
plan_positions.sketch: Institutional landlords, rent-setting algorithms, and short-term rentals turned homes into assets; curb investor ownership to restore affordability.

plan_positions.name: Tenant Decommodifier
plan_positions.sketch: Market housing will never serve the bottom; rent regulation, public and social housing, and tenant power are the real fix.

plan_positions.name: Demand-Side Skeptic
plan_positions.sketch: Income growth and inequality, not regulation, drive price divergence; new market-rate supply won't filter down far or fast enough.

plan_positions.name: Georgist Land Taxer
plan_positions.sketch: The crisis is a land crisis: tax land values instead of buildings to end speculation and reward construction.
